title: The Logic of Persuasion
text:
An argumentative essay sets out to persuade the reader that a particular position is the most defensible one. Unlike a purely descriptive text, it must anticipate objections and respond to them with evidence and reasoning. Writers typically open with a clear thesis, then develop several claims that support it. Although many students regard the form as formulaic, its strength lies in forcing the writer to confront the strongest counterarguments.

The counterargument section is often the most revealing part of such an essay. By acknowledging an opposing view fairly before refuting it, the writer signals intellectual honesty and gains the reader's trust. Weak essays, by contrast, dismiss opposing views with caricature, which tends to alienate readers who already hold them. Consequently, instructors frequently assess how convincingly a writer handles concessions rather than how forcefully they assert their own opinion.

questions.text: According to the first paragraph, what must an argumentative essay do?
options: Describe a place or object in detail
Persuade the reader that a position is the most defensible
Tell a personal story in chronological order
List facts without giving an opinion

questions.text: According to the second paragraph, what do weak essays do with opposing views?
What can be inferred about the writer's approach in a strong essay?
options: They avoid mentioning any opposing position
They treat opponents fairly even while disagreeing with them
They rely mainly on their personal emotions
They try to win by repeating their thesis

questions.text: Why, according to the passage, do instructors often focus on concessions?
options: Because concessions are easier to grade
Because they reveal how well the writer engages with other views
Because they replace the need for a thesis
Because they usually contain the strongest evidence

vocabulary.definition: able to be supported by good reasons and evidence
reasons or arguments against a position
following a fixed pattern, without originality
an exaggerated and distorted version of someone's view

paragraph_translations: Um ensaio argumentativo procura persuadir o leitor de que uma determinada posição é a mais defensável. Ao contrário de um texto puramente descritivo, deve antecipar objeções e responder-lhes com provas e raciocínio. Os autores normalmente começam com uma tese clara e depois desenvolvem várias afirmações que a apoiam. Embora muitos estudantes considerem a forma formulaica, a sua força reside em obrigar o autor a confrontar os contra-argumentos mais fortes.

A secção de contra-argumentos é frequentemente a parte mais reveladora de um ensaio desse tipo. Ao reconhecer com justiça uma visão oposta antes de a refutar, o autor demonstra honestidade intelectual e ganha a confiança do leitor. Em contrapartida, os ensaios fracos rejeitam as posições contrárias com caricaturas, o que tende a afastar os leitores que já as defendem. Por isso, os professores avaliam frequentemente a forma como o autor lida com as concessões, e não apenas a força com que afirma a sua própria opinião.
